title: Reginald's Rotten Tomatoes
markdown:
The air in Mrs. Higgins’s greenhouse hummed with the promise of summer, a low thrum like a contented bumblebee. Rows of tomato plants filled the glass house, plump and heavy, leafy arms reaching for the roof. The leaves caught the sunlight and turned it into a thousand tiny emeralds. This was the day Reginald, the celebrated (in his own mind, at least) rodent photographer, meant to fulfil a promise. The fruit was ripe. The sun had a schedule. So, he believed, did he.

“Bram, old chap, observe,” Reginald declared, his voice a high chirp that bounced off the panes. His paw trembled with excitement. His whiskers twitched like tiny antennae, picking up the sweet earthy scent and the faint metallic tang of the greenhouse frame. Reginald believed that if something was worth doing, it was worth diagramming. Spread across a potting bench already dusted with fine soil was a sprawling blueprint: levers, pulleys, an elaborate collection chute, all designed to harvest a perfectly blemish-free haul of tomatoes by sunset. Each line was drawn with the care of a cartographer charting a new continent.

Bram, a badger of few and well-chosen words, peered at the diagram. His brow, a ridge of soft grey fur, furrowed. “Reginald,” he rumbled, like pebbles shifting in a stream, “that’s a lot of lines for a few tomatoes.” He nudged a stray scrap with his snout, so gently the dust barely moved. Bram had learned long ago that the simplest path was often the wisest.

“Nonsense, my dear Bram,” Reginald squeaked, soaring with the conviction of a scientist on the cusp of a breakthrough. “Perfection requires precision. This machine,” he patted a large whirring assembly of polished brass and repurposed garden tools, “will ensure each tomato is plucked with the utmost care, catalogued, and presented flawlessly. Mrs. Higgins awaits a truly magnificent harvest, and I, Reginald, shall deliver.” He had promised this with a flourish of his camera lens and a dramatic bow, some weeks prior, on a particularly bright afternoon. He had built the machine from the diagram alone, connecting each piece with a scholar’s focus. When he finally flipped the switch, the lever gave a satisfying clunk. It worked. Gears spun with a delightful whir. Levers lifted with balletic grace. The collection chute swooped in an elegant arc.

Then the first tomatoes were plucked, and, with a soft unmistakable sploosh, a burst of crimson pulp sprayed across the gleaming brass. The collection chute, designed for delicate handling, was a very efficient tomato pulverizer. It was not picking. It was processing.

“Oh, whiskers and woebegone,” Reginald wailed. His paws flew to his face. A cascade of crimson tumbled into the collection bin. The machine, a triumph of engineering, was a disaster for produce. It was like building a grand opera house and then only being able to play a kazoo inside.

Bram shuffled closer. He did not scold. He did not even sigh, which, for Bram, was high praise. He simply nudged a half-squashed tomato with his snout. “It’s rather colourful, isn’t it, Reginald?” The pulp had splattered in a rather artistic pattern on the side of the bin.

Reginald stared. His promise, his reputation, his pride in the work, were splattering before his eyes. He had promised perfection. He had made tomato paste. His shoulders slumped. A profound sigh escaped him. The diagrams had become the obstacle. The perfect plan had led to imperfect, messy results, as jarring as a wrong note in a beautiful melody.

He looked at Bram. The badger was not judging. He was simply there, solid in the middle of the unraveling. The thrill of a perfectly drawn line had blinded Reginald to the simple fact of ripe fruit. The machine worked flawlessly according to its specifications. The specifications were wrong.

“Bram,” Reginald whispered, the drama leaving his voice. “I think I need a different kind of diagram.”

He stopped. For a moment the greenhouse was only itself: warm glass, a bee bumping softly against a pane, the sweet-sour smell of crushed summer. Light caught in the pulp on the brass and made it look, briefly, like stained glass. Reginald breathed until the scent became less offensive and more fragrant — abundance, even if slightly damaged.

Then the second trouble arrived, quieter than the sploosh and harder to diagram. The sun had slid down the roof. Shadows stretched between the rows. Several remaining tomatoes hung too heavy, skins tight, ready to drop. Mrs. Higgins always came at the dipping of the light. There was no time to rebuild the machine, and no time to pretend the pulp could be un-pulped.

Reginald looked at the plants, then at Bram’s steady gaze. With a burst of spontaneity that did not appear on any blueprint, he grabbed a large wicker basket from the corner, its weave worn smooth by use. The mechanical masterpiece was left silently dripping its crimson tears.

“Forget the machine, Bram. Let’s just pick them. We’ll collect what we can, however we can.”

Bram’s quiet smile crinkled the fur around his eyes. He began gathering fallen tomatoes, the ones the machine had missed, the ones that had rolled gently to the ground. Reginald, surprisingly agile for a rat so accustomed to the drawing board, began carefully plucking the remaining ripe ones. The skins were sun-warm and slightly dusty. Juice found his paws. He placed each fruit in the basket. The soft thud of tomato against tomato was a far simpler, more honest sound than the whirring of the contraption. They worked together, the dramatic rat and the sensible badger, a dance of improvisation, racing the gold as it left the glass.

By the time the sun dipped below the greenhouse roof, the harvest was far from perfect. There were squashed ones, bruised ones, and some gently mangled by Reginald’s earlier masterpiece. There were also many perfectly good, sun-warmed tomatoes, glowing with the last of the day.

When Mrs. Higgins arrived, her face a picture of gentle curiosity, Reginald braced himself. “Mrs. Higgins,” he began, voice steady, “about the harvest…”

She looked at the basket, a colourful jumble of red and orange. She looked at the dismantled, slightly sticky machine. She looked at Reginald and Bram, earnest. A slow smile spread across her face. “Oh, Reginald,” she chuckled, warm as sunshine. “You always do make things interesting. These slightly squashed ones? They make the most divine sauce. And look.” She pointed to a particularly plump tomato, slightly misshapen but wonderfully red, its curves almost heart-like. “This one looks like a little heart. How poetic.”

Reginald’s whiskers gave a small shy twitch. He looked at the basket, then at Bram, who gave him a knowing nod. For the first time he did not feel the need to draw a diagram of what happened next. He kept one slightly squashed tomato. The machine was destined for the scrap heap. That evening the kept tomato sat on his bench, catching the last of the greenhouse gold, and needed no catalogue number at all.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
